The Banded studfish (Fundulus diaphanus) is a small-bodied cyprinodontiform fish that inhabits freshwater systems across eastern North America. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal eggs at an extremely modest size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0109 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0109 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter documented in a congener. This diminutive starting mass underscores the vulnerability of the earliest larval stages, which rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the endotrophic phase before mouth opening and first exogenous feeding. The initial growth trajectory is rapid, though it is highly contingent upon thermal conditions and food availability within the shallow, vegetated littoral zones this species frequents. Field collections and laboratory-rearing studies have shown that individuals can attain a body length of 9.5 centimeters [Li = 9.5 centimeters] under optimal conditions, representing the ultimate standard length for the species. This asymptotic size is typical for a fundulid of moderate body plan, reflecting a life history strategy that balances early maturation with sustained somatic investment.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is readily apparent in Fundulus diaphanus, as males do not attain the same maximum dimensions as females. Data from preserved museum series and field surveys indicate that the ultimate standard length for males is 5.9 centimeters [Li = 5.9 centimeters], a considerably smaller value than that recorded for females. This disparity may be linked to differential energetic allocation, with females investing more heavily in somatic growth to accommodate greater fecundity, while males may channel resources into reproductive behaviors such as territorial defense and fin display. The onset of reproductive capability is marked by the attainment of puberty, which occurs at a total length of 3.7 centimeters [Lp = 3.7 centimeters]. Individuals reaching this size threshold are capable of initiating gametogenesis and participating in the spawning population, although the first spawning event may be deferred depending on local environmental conditions and the timing of the breeding season.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic summer thermal regimes. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 2.9 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2.9 eggs per day]. This elevated spawning intensity reflects the compressed breeding window typical of temperate fundulids, during which females can produce multiple clutches in rapid succession. The fecundity per reproductive event averages approximately 15 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 15 eggs per clutch], and the frequency of those events reaches roughly 0.19 clutches per day [F_R_i = roughly 0.19 clutches per day] under those same thermal conditions. This sustained reproductive effort, while energetically demanding, allows the population to offset the high natural mortality experienced during the early larval phase.

Adult body mass provides another axis of sexual differentiation. The ultimate wet weight for females can reach up to 8.2 grams [Wwi = up to 8.2 grams], a value consistent with the larger standard length documented for that sex. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males is substantially lower at 1.99 grams [Wwi = 1.99 grams], reflecting their smaller somatic dimensions. This fourfold difference in maximum body mass between the sexes is more pronounced than the length dimorphism would suggest, indicating that females are not only longer but also deeper-bodied, likely an adaptation for accommodating the developing oocyte mass during the spawning season. The weight-length relationship in this species exhibits positive allometry, with gravid females showing a disproportionately rapid gain in mass relative to length during the reproductive period.

Longevity in Fundulus diaphanus is modest, as is typical for small-bodied annual or short-lived iteroparous fishes. Under natural conditions, individuals are believed to survive a maximum of approximately 1,168 days [am = approximately 1,168 days] from birth when exposed to an average ambient temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This value, equivalent to roughly 3.2 years, aligns with field observations that few individuals persist beyond their second or third spawning season. The physiological mechanisms underlying senescence in this species are not well studied, but it is probable that the cumulative energetic costs of repeated reproduction, combined with seasonal metabolic stress and predation pressure, contribute to the relatively short natural lifespan. Compared to congeners occupying more stable thermal environments, the lifespan of F. diaphanus appears to be constrained by the cold winters and variable water levels that characterize its native range.
